content: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis and Yersinia enterocolitica Enterocolitis Treatment: There is no evidence that early antimicrobial therapy reduces the frequency or severity of chronic sequelae for infections caused by Y. enterocolitica or Y. pseudotuberculosis. These organisms are susceptible to ampicillin, third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, and chloramphenicol. Septicemia Treatment: The preferred regimen is ceftriaxone 1 g IM/IV every 12 hours. For pediatric patients, the dose is ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day (up to 2 g/day) IM/IV every 12 hours. The duration of treatment is not well-established, but some Yersinia infections have been treated for at least three weeks. Yersinia pestis (Plague) Plague Treatment: Preferred Regimen 1: Streptomycin 2 g/day IM every 12 hours for at least 10 days. For pediatric patients, the dose is 30 mg/kg/day (up to 2 g/day) IM every 6–12 hours for at least 10 days. Preferred Regimen 2: Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IM or IV every 8 hours for at least 10 days. For neonates/infants, use 7.5 mg/kg/day. Alternative Regimens: Chloramphenicol 50 mg/kg/day IV or PO every 6 hours for 10 days. Tetracycline 2 g/day PO in divided doses (qid) for 10 days. Pediatric dose: 15 mg/kg loading dose, then 25–50 mg/kg/day (up to 2 g/day) PO in divided doses (qid) for 10 days. Sulfadiazine 2–4 g loading dose, then 1 g PO every 4–6 hours. Doxycycline 200 mg/day PO every 12–24 hours. Notes: Fluoroquinolones have shown good efficacy against Y. pestis in vitro and in animal studies, but no human studies have been published. Other antibiotics have been shown to be ineffective against plague. Plague Prophylaxis: Preferred Regimen: Tetracycline 1–2 g/day PO in divided doses (bid–qid). Pediatric dose: 25–50 mg/kg/day (up to 2 g/day) PO in divided doses (qid) for 10 days. Alternative Regimens: Doxycycline 100–200 mg/day PO every 12–24 hours. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim 1.6 g/day PO in divided doses (bid). Pediatric dose: 40 mg/kg/day PO in divided doses (bid). Neutropenic Fever Empiric Initial Treatment: Low-Risk Patients (anticipated neutropenia <7 days, clinically stable, no medical comorbidities, MASCC score ≥21): Preferred regimen is ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate. High-Risk Patients (anticipated neutropenia >7 days, clinically unstable, or with medical comorbidities, MASCC score <21): Preferred regimens include: 1. Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours. 2. Imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours. 3. Meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours. 4. Cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours. 5. Ceftazidime 2 g IV every 8 hours. Alternative regimens for penicillin-allergic patients: 1. Ciprofloxacin plus clindamycin. 2. Aztreonam plus vancomycin. Notes: Monotherapy is preferred as no study has shown superiority for combination therapy. Add vancomycin if the patient has signs of severe sepsis, hemodynamic instability, pneumonia, positive blood cultures for gram-positive bacteria, suspected central venous catheter-related infection, skin or soft tissue infection, or severe mucositis in patients receiving prophylaxis with a fluoroquinolone lacking activity against streptococci. Modify the initial regimen if the patient is at risk of infection with antibiotic-resistant organisms (e.g., MRSA, VRE, ESBLs, KPCs). Do not change the initial regimen due to unexplained persistent fever if the patient is stable. However, if an infection is identified, treat accordingly. If vancomycin or other gram-positive coverage was started initially, it may be stopped after 2–3 days if there is no evidence of a gram-positive infection. Empiric antifungal coverage should be considered in high-risk neutropenic patients with persistent fever after 4–7 days of broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy and no identified source of fever.
